Herbert Hoover. The thirty-first President of the United States, serving from nineteen-twenty-nine to nineteen-thirty-three. His administration collided catastrophically with the Great Depression, defining his presidency as a failure of leadership. A successful mining engineer and humanitarian relief coordinator during World War One, Hoover entered office as a cautious Republican at the moment the stock market crashed. His belief in limited government and refusal to implement aggressive federal relief made him seem callous to a nation in crisis, leading to his landslide defeat by Franklin D. Roosevelt in the election of nineteen-thirty-two.

Hoover began his presidency in March nineteen-twenty-nine, just eight months before the stock market crash of October that triggered the Great Depression. He believed that excessive government intervention would weaken American self-reliance and capitalism, and he favored voluntary business cooperation over federal programs. He supported the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of nineteen-thirty, which raised import duties and is widely blamed for worsening international trade collapse and deepening the Depression.

He authorized limited relief through the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to prop up banks and railroads, but resisted direct aid to unemployed individuals. He largely rejected calls for public works programs and welfare expansion, a position that became politically toxic as unemployment exceeded twenty-five percent. He lost the nineteen-thirty-two election to Franklin D. Roosevelt in a landslide, ending Republican electoral dominance and ushering in the New Deal era.

Hoover lived until nineteen-sixty-four, but his reputation never recovered. Hoovervilles, shantytowns of the homeless, became a bitter monument to his name.
